Similarity Between Feature Sets

Source: R/metrics.R
stabl_similarity.Rd

Computes the similarity between two sets of selected features, or between all pairs of sets in a list, using one of three methods. Use this to assess the reproducibility of STABL (or any other feature-selection method) across cross-validation folds or repeated runs.

Usage

stabl_similarity(
  x,
  y = NULL,
  method = c("jaccard", "adjusted", "pearson"),
  n_universe = NULL,
  as_matrix = FALSE,
  remove_diag = FALSE
)

Arguments

x

Either a character/integer vector of selected feature identifiers (then y must also be supplied and the result is a single scalar), or a list of such vectors, one per STABL run (then y must be NULL and all pairwise similarities are computed).

y

NULL (default) or a character/integer vector of selected feature identifiers. Supply y for scalar mode, or a list as x for pairwise mode — not both.

method

Character; one of "jaccard" (default), "adjusted", or "pearson".

n_universe

Integer; total number of candidate features in the universe (i.e. the number of columns in the original predictor matrix). Required for method = "adjusted" and method = "pearson"; ignored for method = "jaccard".

as_matrix

Logical; pairwise mode only. If FALSE (default), returns the \(N (N - 1) / 2\) off-diagonal upper-triangle values as a flat vector in row-major order (matching the Python convention). If TRUE, returns the full symmetric \(N \times N\) matrix.

remove_diag

Logical; only used when as_matrix = TRUE. If TRUE the self-similarity diagonal is removed row-wise, yielding an \(N \times (N - 1)\) matrix in which row \(i\) contains the similarities of run \(i\) with every other run.

Value

In scalar mode, a numeric scalar. In pairwise mode with as_matrix = FALSE, a numeric vector of length \(N (N - 1) / 2\). In pairwise mode with as_matrix = TRUE, a numeric matrix of dimension \(N \times N\) (or \(N \times (N - 1)\) when remove_diag = TRUE).

The matrix diagonal holds the self-similarity of each set: exactly 1 for "jaccard" and "pearson", and the computed self-value for "adjusted" (\(1 - k / d\) for a set of size \(k \le d / 2\)), which is below 1 by construction because the measure is chance-corrected.

Details

Three methods are available:

"jaccard" (default)

Set-overlap fraction \(|A \cap B| / |A \cup B|\). The most interpretable measure; it does not correct for the chance overlap expected between small or large sets. When both sets are empty the value is 0 (convention matching the Python implementation).

"adjusted"

Chance-corrected overlap, analogous to Cohen's kappa for sets: $$S_{\text{adj}}(A, B) = \frac{r - \mathbb{E}[r]}{\min(k_1, k_2) - \max(0, k_1 + k_2 - d)}$$ where \(r = |A \cap B|\), \(k_i = |A_i|\), \(d =\) n_universe, and \(\mathbb{E}[r] = k_1 k_2 / d\). Returns 0 when either set is empty or equals the full universe.

"pearson"

Pearson-correlation-inspired chance correction (the phi coefficient): $$S_{\text{Pearson}}(A, B) = \frac{r - k_i k_j / d}{d \cdot \upsilon_i \upsilon_j}$$ with \(\upsilon_i = \sqrt{\pi_i (1 - \pi_i)}\) and \(\pi_i = k_i / d\). Returns 1 when both sets are empty or both equal the universe; 0 when exactly one of them is.

See also

stabl_similarity_summary() for reducing pairwise values to a single location statistic.

Examples

# Scalar mode: two sets
stabl_similarity(c("A", "B", "C"), c("B", "C", "D"))                # 0.5
#> [1] 0.5
stabl_similarity(c("f1", "f2", "f3"), c("f2", "f3", "f4"),
                 method = "adjusted", n_universe = 10L)
#> [1] 0.3666667

# Pairwise mode: a list of sets, one per run
sets <- list(c("f1", "f2", "f3"), c("f2", "f3", "f4"), c("f1", "f3", "f5"))
stabl_similarity(sets)                                        # flat vector
#> [1] 0.5 0.5 0.2
stabl_similarity(sets, as_matrix = TRUE)                      # 3 x 3
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]  1.0  0.5  0.5
#> [2,]  0.5  1.0  0.2
#> [3,]  0.5  0.2  1.0
stabl_similarity(sets, as_matrix = TRUE, remove_diag = TRUE)  # 3 x 2
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]  0.5  0.5
#> [2,]  0.5  0.2
#> [3,]  0.5  0.2
stabl_similarity(sets, method = "adjusted", n_universe = 10L)
#> [1] 0.36666667 0.36666667 0.03333333
